verses.1: A psalm. A song for the day of the Sabbath.
verses.2: It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praise to your name, Most High.
verses.3: To declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness through the nights,
verses.4: with ten-stringed lyre and with music, with the harp.
verses.5: For you have made me glad, O LORD, in your works; in the deeds of your hands I will rejoice.
verses.6: How great are your works, O LORD! How deeply profound are your thoughts!
verses.7: A foolish man does not understand this, and a silly man does not grasp it.
verses.8: When the wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish, it is that they may be destroyed forever.
verses.9: But you, O LORD, are most high forever.
verses.10: For behold, your enemies, O LORD, behold, your enemies will perish; all evildoers will be scattered.
verses.11: But my horn you have lifted up like a wild ox; I have been anointed with fresh oil.
verses.12: My eyes have seen my enemies; my ears have heard the wicked rising up against me.
verses.13: The righteous will flourish like the date palm, like a cedar in Lebanon they will grow.
verses.14: Planted in the house of the LORD, in the courts of our God they will flourish.
verses.15: They will still bear fruit in old age; they will remain fresh and green,
verses.16: to declare that the LORD is upright; there is no injustice in him.

notes:
Notes  
- v. 8: "it is that they may be destroyed forever" — the Hebrew uses poetic causality (כְּלַל) to express purpose, not merely result.  
- v. 9: "most high" — the Hebrew uses an emphatic form of *eleyyon* ("Most High"), not a direct synonym for *Elohim*, to retain the poetic contrast with the wicked.  
- v. 11: "wild ox" — the Hebrew *kerem* is often translated "unicorn" in older versions, but "wild ox" is a more natural rendering in English and fits the imagery of strength and majesty.

[9] But you, O LORD, are most high forever.

Notes  
- v. 8: "it is that they may be destroyed forever" — the Hebrew uses poetic causality (כְּלַל) to express purpose, not merely result.  
- v. 9: "most high" — the Hebrew uses an emphatic form of *eleyyon* ("Most High"), not a direct synonym for *Elohim*, to retain the poetic contrast with the wicked.
